item.title: UT Austin physicists confirm 1970s 2D magnetism theory
item.description: Physicists at the University of Texas at Austin have experimentally demonstrated the full sequence of exotic magnetic phases predicted by a theoretical model of two-dimensional magnetism first proposed in the 1970s, marking the first time the complete framework has been realized in a real material. The results were published in the journal Nature Materials.

item.title: Israel's Iron Beam laser utilised in combat for first time
item.description: Israel's Iron Beam laser defense system saw its first operational use in combat early Monday as it helped intercept aerial threats launched by Hezbollah from Lebanon, marking a milestone for directed-energy weapons in warfare. The deployment came as the Middle East plunged deeper into crisis following the assassination of Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei in a joint U.S.-Israeli strike on February 28.

item.title: China set to lower growth target as parliament opens
item.description: China is poised to trim its economic growth target for the first time in four years when Premier Li Qiang delivers the government work report at the opening of the National People's Congress on March 5. Most analysts expect Beijing to set a 2026 GDP growth target of 4.5% to 5%, a step down from the "around 5%" goal maintained over the past three years.

item.title: India cuts industrial gas supply after Qatar halts LNG production
item.description:
Indian energy companies on Tuesday slashed natural gas deliveries to industrial consumers by 10 to 30 percent after Qatar — the country's largest supplier of liquefied natural gas — halted all LNG production following Iranian drone strikes on two major facilities.

Petronet LNG, India's top LNG importer, notified GAIL, the leading gas marketing firm, and other companies of reduced supplies late Monday, according to Reuters, citing four industry sources. GAIL and Indian Oil Corporation then relayed the cuts to their downstream customers.

item.title: Asian shares fall as Iran war chokes global oil supply
item.description:
The U.S.-Israeli military campaign against Iran, now entering its fourth day, has sent shockwaves through global energy and financial markets, with oil prices surging, the Strait of Hormuz effectively shut to commercial shipping, and investors scrambling for safe-haven assets.

Brent crude spiked as much as 13% over the weekend before settling around $79 per barrel on Monday, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude jumped roughly 8%. Analysts at Barclays and Rystad Energy have warned that prices could reach $100 a barrel if disruptions persist. On Tuesday in Asia, oil prices continued climbing, with Brent adding another $1.10 to near $79.

item.title: IAEA confirms damage at Iran's Natanz nuclear site
item.description:
The International Atomic Energy Agency confirmed on Tuesday that entrance buildings at Iran's underground Natanz Fuel Enrichment Plant sustained damage during the ongoing U.S.-Israeli military campaign, but said no radiological consequences are expected.

"Based on the latest available satellite imagery, IAEA can now confirm some recent damage to entrance buildings of Iran's underground Natanz Fuel Enrichment Plant (FEP)," the agency wrote on X. "No radiological consequence expected and no additional impact detected at FEP itself, which was severely damaged in the June conflict."

item.title: Oil tops $82 as Iran conflict threatens Strait of Hormuz
item.description:
Oil prices surged to their highest levels since early 2025 this week as an expanding military conflict between the United States and Israel on one side and Iran on the other rattled global energy markets and raised fears of prolonged supply disruptions through the Strait of Hormuz.

Brent crude closed Monday's session up roughly 6.7%, after earlier spiking as much as 13% to above $82 per barrel — its highest point since January 2025, according to Reuters. U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude also climbed more than 6% on Monday. By Tuesday, prices continued to rise, with Brent topping $82 a barrel as concerns mounted over the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

item.title: Bank of Japan may delay rate hike as Iran war roils markets
item.description:
The war between the United States, Israel, and Iran has sent shockwaves through global energy and financial markets, with crude oil prices surging and investors scrambling for safe-haven assets as the conflict enters its fourth day with no sign of de-escalation.

Brent crude, the international benchmark, spiked as much as 13% over the weekend before settling with gains of roughly 9% on Monday, climbing into the upper $70s per barrel. The surge came as the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps effectively shut down the Strait of Hormuz, a chokepoint through which roughly 20% of the world's daily oil supply passes. Tanker traffic through the strait dropped to near zero, with more than 150 ships anchoring outside to avoid the risks.

item.title: Researchers use 270-year-old physics trick to build longer-lasting sodium batteries
item.description: An international team of scientists has harnessed a centuries-old physics phenomenon to build a sodium-ion battery cathode that lasts over 10,000 charge-discharge cycles, a development that could help wean large-scale energy storage off scarce lithium. The study, published in the journal Small, brings together researchers from India's IISER Bhopal and IIT Gandhinagar, Swansea University in the UK, and the University of Southern Queensland in Australia.

item.title: US closes embassies in Kuwait and Saudi Arabia amid Iranian drone strikes
item.description:
The U.S. Embassy in Kuwait was struck by at least one drone on Monday, sparking a large fire at the compound and prompting the mission to close indefinitely as Iran's retaliatory attacks against American interests in the Gulf entered a third consecutive day.

Three diplomatic sources confirmed to AFP that the embassy compound in Kuwait City was hit by drones on March 2, with smoke seen billowing from the area. No injuries were reported, according to a U.S. official, and staff had been ordered to return to their residences and shelter in place before the fire broke out, leaving few if any employees inside the main building at the time.

item.title: Israel sends ground forces into southern Lebanon amid Hezbollah clashes
item.description:
Israeli troops crossed into southern Lebanon on Tuesday, seizing new positions beyond the border as the military expanded its campaign against Hezbollah following days of rocket and drone attacks that have opened a second front in the broader U.S.-Israeli war against Iran.

The Israel Defense Forces said soldiers from the 91st "Galilee" Division entered southern Lebanon and captured several strategic points as part of what the military called an "enhanced forward defense posture," moving beyond five outposts Israel has maintained since a ceasefire was reached in November 2024. Eyewitnesses told Xinhua that an Israeli force including a tank and three military bulldozers crossed the Blue Line at around 8:00 a.m. local time, advancing roughly one kilometer into Lebanese territory near the town of Tal al-Nahas.

item.title: Russia's Medvedev warns of World War III over US strikes on Iran
item.description: As U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran entered their fourth day, Russia's Security Council Deputy Chairman Dmitry Medvedev warned that World War III "will undoubtedly begin" if President Donald Trump "continues his insane course of criminally changing political regimes," while analysts said the widening conflict is undermining Washington's ability to deter China in the Pacific.

item.title: Hardy bacterium survives Mars-like asteroid blast in lab
item.description:
A resilient desert bacterium survived pressures equivalent to being blasted off the surface of Mars by an asteroid strike, according to a new study from Johns Hopkins University, lending fresh support to the idea that life could travel between planets aboard space debris.

The research, published Monday in PNAS Nexus, found that the extremophile Deinococcus radiodurans — a bacterium found in the high deserts of Chile — achieved nearly 100% survival at 1.4 Gigapascals of pressure and 60% survival at 2.4 Gigapascals, far exceeding what scientists had thought possible. By comparison, other commonly studied microorganisms such as E. coli and Shewanella oneidensis showed survival rates below 10% at similar pressures.

item.title: IAEA says no nuclear sites hit in Iran strikes as Tehran alleges Natanz was targeted
item.description:
The head of the International Atomic Energy Agency told an emergency board meeting on Monday that the agency has found no evidence Iran is developing nuclear weapons, even as he warned that ongoing U.S. and Israeli military strikes risk triggering a radiological disaster.

IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi addressed the agency's 35-nation Board of Governors in Vienna on March 2, convened at Russia's request following the launch of Operation Roaring Lion — a coordinated U.S.-Israeli military campaign against Iran that began on February 28. Grossi told the board that the IAEA has "no indication" that any nuclear installations in Iran, "including the Bushehr Nuclear Power Plant, the Tehran Research Reactor, or other nuclear fuel cycle facilities have been damaged or hit".

item.title: Trump open to arming militias inside Iran, officials say
item.description:
President Trump is open to backing armed groups inside Iran willing to fight the Islamic regime, U.S. officials told The Wall Street Journal on Monday, a move that would deepen American involvement in a conflict that has already killed Iran's supreme leader and drawn the U.S. into its largest Middle Eastern military operation in two decades.

The revelation came as Trump spoke by phone on Sunday with the leaders of Iraq's two main Kurdish factions — Masoud Barzani and Bafel Talabani — to discuss the war and what might come next, according to Axios, which first reported the calls. Kurdish forces maintain thousands of troops along the Iran-Iraq border and have deep ties with Iran's Kurdish minority. The outreach was driven in part by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who has long cultivated relationships with Kurdish groups and raised their potential role during a meeting with Trump at the White House, Axios reported.

item.title: Dow drops over 1,000 points as Iran conflict roils markets
item.description:
A wave of selling swept through global equity markets on Monday and Tuesday as the U.S.-Israel military campaign against Iran entered its fourth day with no sign of de-escalation, rattling investors with fears of prolonged energy disruption and a fresh surge in inflation.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average plunged more than 1,000 points on Tuesday, March 3 — on pace for its largest single-day drop since April 2025, according to The Wall Street Journal. The S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100 futures fell 1.5% and 1.9%, respectively, in pre-market trading Tuesday. A day earlier, U.S. stocks had staged a late-session recovery, with the S&P 500 finishing nearly flat and the Nasdaq Composite gaining 0.4%, after initially dropping more than 1%.

item.title: Indian team hits 30.2% efficiency in perovskite-silicon solar cell
item.description: A wave of recent breakthroughs in perovskite solar cell research is bringing the promising but fragile technology closer to commercial viability, with teams across Asia and Europe reporting new methods to boost both efficiency and long-term stability in tandem perovskite-silicon devices.

item.title: Dow sinks as oil surges on Iran's Strait of Hormuz shutdown
item.description:
Oil prices soared for a third consecutive day on Tuesday and stocks tumbled sharply as the war between the United States and Iran entered its fourth day, with tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz at a near standstill and no signs of a quick resolution to the conflict.

West Texas Intermediate crude climbed roughly 8% to around $76.91 per barrel, while Brent crude jumped about 7.6% to $83.65, its highest level since mid-2024, according to CNN. The Dow Jones Industrial Average sank more than 1,000 points in early trading, while the S&P 500 fell over 2% and the Nasdaq Composite dropped by a similar margin.

item.title: Apple unveils six devices in two days, more expected
item.description:
Apple has announced six new products over two days in its most aggressive spring launch in years, with at least one more device expected when the company hosts media at a hands-on "experience" event on Wednesday.

The announcements began Monday, March 2, with the iPhone 17e and the M4 iPad Air, followed Tuesday by the M5 MacBook Air, M5 Pro and M5 Max MacBook Pro, and a pair of new Studio Displays. Pre-orders for most of the new hardware open March 4, with availability beginning March 11.

item.title: SpaceX's Starship faces 5-month launch gap as IPO filing nears
item.description:
SpaceX has gone nearly five months without a Starship launch — the longest pause since the program's early days — even as the company prepares to file paperwork for what could become the largest initial public offering in history.

The world's largest rocket last flew on October 13, 2025, when Flight 11 closed out a year of five test missions. As of early March, no official launch date has been set for Flight 12, and the mission does not appear on SpaceX's online schedule. Elon Musk suggested in a January 26 post on X that the next launch was six weeks away, pointing to a March liftoff, but that timeline has not been confirmed by the company.
